# Distributed Training and Sharding

Also called: Distributed 3DGS, Multi-GPU Sharding

## Overview
Distributed training and sharding partition the global set of 3D Gaussians $\mathcal{G}$ and optimizer states across $M$ GPUs to enable city-scale optimization that exceeds single-GPU memory and compute limits [S2, unofficial]. Unlike spatial block partitioning, which suffers from cross-block visibility waste, imbalanced shards, and expensive merge steps, BlitzGS uses index-parity sharding combined with all-to-all communication to route Gaussians to responsible tiles, ensuring balanced loads without final merging [S2, unofficial].

## Shared principles
See [Hardware and Computational Acceleration](16214-hardware-and-computational-acceleration.md) for the shared rendering pipeline principles.

## Subtopics

### BlitzGS
BlitzGS is a distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework designed to accelerate city-scale training by reducing the active Gaussian workload at three coupled levels: system-level sharding, model-level population control, and view-level filtering [S2, unofficial]. Unlike spatial block partitioning which suffers from cross-block visibility waste and imbalanced shards, BlitzGS shards Gaussians by index parity and uses a single all-to-all communication step to distribute rendering tiles, ensuring balanced loads without a final merge step [S2, unofficial]. It achieves nearly an order-of-magnitude speedup over an edge GPU baseline (5.41×) and up to 17.3× with a customized accelerator, while incurring minimal visual quality degradation [S1].

### [GS-Cache Inference Framework](15588-gs-cache-inference-framework.md)
GS-Cache is a holistic rendering framework designed to support real-time rendering of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models at the city level, achieving >72 FPS at binocular 2K resolution. It addresses the computational bottleneck of the "Gaussian Derivation Stage" in structured Gaussian methods (e.g., Scaffold-GS, Octree-GS) by employing a cache-centric de-redundancy pipeline. Unlike native 3DGS or unstructured methods, GS-Cache specifically targets structured representations where anchors derive neural Gaussians, optimizing inter-frame redundancy in parameter decoding while maintaining rasterization quality.

### LS-Gaussian Accelerator Architecture
**Definition:** A hardware architecture co-designed with the LS-Gaussian algorithm to support workload-aware mapping, featuring a streaming pipeline that allows continuous processing across hardware modules without requiring global synchronization [S1].
**Step:** The accelerator predicts the workload for each tile based on viewpoint transformation to enable more balanced parallel computation [S1].
**Comparison:** Unlike naive assignment of tiles to rendering blocks which fails to achieve balanced load distribution, this architecture uses workload prediction to mitigate inter-block idling and intra-block bubbles [S1].

### Spatial Block Partitioning
**Definition:** Divides the scene into fixed world-space spatial blocks (e.g., uniform grid) [S2, unofficial].
**Step:** Construct a uniform grid (e.g., 4×5 or 5×6) and assign each block a boundary halo of neighboring Gaussians for cross-block consistency [S2, unofficial]. Each GPU is bound to a specific block and trains its Gaussians independently [S2, unofficial]. During rendering, cameras near block boundaries trigger cross-block visibility overlap and boundary reassignment, requiring a final single-GPU merge to assemble the full scene [S2, unofficial].
**Pitfall:** Overlapping blocks re-optimize the same surfaces, wasting computation [S2, unofficial]. In a 20-block split, 23.5M Gaussians are optimized but only 5.37M survive merge (77% discarded) [S2, unofficial]. Finer partitions increase redundancy and training time with negligible quality gain (<0.2 dB) [S2, unofficial].
**Number:** On Building (1,920 cameras, 4 GPUs), 86.8% of cameras fall in ≥2 blocks for 20-block partition, and 95.5% for 30-block partition [S2, unofficial]. Wall-clock time for split/make-span/merge reaches 115.6–169.8 min vs 39 min for sharding [S2, unofficial].

### Primitive Sharding (Index-Parity Sharding)
**Definition:** Distributes a single global Gaussian model across multiple GPUs by assigning Gaussians to ranks based on index parity [S2, unofficial]. Each GPU holds a balanced, scene-wide slice of the model [S2, unofficial].
**Step:** Assign each Gaussian primitive to a GPU rank using index parity [S2, unofficial]. During rendering, distribute each step through balanced tile allocation across GPUs [S2, unofficial]. Route projected Gaussians to tile owners via all-to-all communication [S2, unofficial]. Train using a single global camera stream [S2, unofficial]. Each camera enters training once per iteration with no cross-block duplication [S2, unofficial]. Only distributed cost is the all-to-all exchange inside each render step [S2, unofficial].
**Number:** On a 4-GPU setup (Building scene, 1,920 cameras), communication cost for routing projected Gaussians to tile owners is 3–5 ms per iteration, staying under 7% of total iteration time [S2, unofficial].
**Comparison:** Unlike spatial block partitioning, it eliminates boundary reassignment, cross-block visibility overlap, and the final single-GPU merge step [S2, unofficial]. Storage and per-step rendering remain evenly distributed as GPU count grows [S2, unofficial].

### [Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting](16979-distributed-3d-gaussian-splatting.md)
**Definition:** A multi-GPU extension of the 3D-GS pipeline designed for scientific visualization, enabling scalable processing of large datasets that exceed single-GPU memory capacity.
**Step:** Partition the global set of Gaussian primitives and training data across multiple GPUs. Utilize a fused all-reduce scheme for gradient synchronization to maintain high-fidelity isosurface reconstruction at previously infeasible scales.
**When to choose:** Use when training on scientific volume data (e.g., CFD simulations) with Gaussian counts exceeding ~11.2M, which exceeds the memory limit of a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.

### [Distributed Batched Rendering Loop](18495-distributed-batched-rendering-loop.md)
**Definition:** A parallelized training and inference pipeline for 3DGS that processes multiple camera views simultaneously across a cluster of GPUs.
**Step:** Partition the global set of 3D Gaussians and distribute the rendering workload. Employ dynamic load balancing and sparse all-to-all communication to ensure efficient data distribution and aggregation across distributed ranks.
**When to choose:** Use to solve memory and compute bottlenecks of single-GPU training for high-resolution and large-scale scene reconstruction.

### [Online Image Rendering Placement](19195-online-image-rendering-placement.md)
**Definition:** A per-iteration optimization step in distributed 3DGS training that assigns image patches to GPUs to minimize inter-node communication and balance computational load.
**Step:** Dynamically solve for the optimal data placement for each small training batch using a fast heuristic solver, rather than relying on offline pre-computed assignments.
**When to choose:** Use when scaling to many GPUs where whole-image assignment limits flexibility, and patch-level granularity (p=2–8) is needed for fine-grained placement.

### [Grendel](19770-grendel.md)
**Definition:** A distributed training system for 3DGS that partitions parameters and parallelizes computation across multiple GPUs to overcome single-GPU memory constraints in high-resolution and large-scale reconstruction.
**Step:** Support batched training with multiple views and exploit mixed parallelism (Gaussian-wise and pixel-wise) with sparse all-to-all communication to handle dynamic workload imbalances.
**When to choose:** Use when static workload partitioning fails due to dynamic and unbalanced workloads caused by varying Gaussian densities and scene complexity.

## Background
Originating from the need to scale 3D Gaussian Splatting to city-scale scenes, distributed training methods evolved from naive spatial partitioning to sophisticated index-parity sharding [S2, unofficial]. Spatial block partitioning was found to be inefficient due to boundary overlaps and merge costs [S2, unofficial]. BlitzGS introduced index-parity sharding to eliminate these issues, achieving significant speedups [S2, unofficial]. Concurrently, LS-Gaussian focused on hardware-aware streaming and workload prediction to reduce stalls in real-time rendering [S1].
